# Part VIII: Safety, Interpretability, and Governance {#part-safety .unnumbered}

> "... an in-depth understanding of the potential risks posed by these models is
> needed."
>
> Laura Weidinger et al., ["Ethical and social risks of harm from Language Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04359)

Safety is not one layer at the top of the stack. It is a set of questions that
return at every boundary: what the model is doing internally, who can oversee it,
which tools it may use, what policy applies at runtime, how it behaves under
attack, what it remembers, and who is accountable when the system causes harm.
This part collects those questions after the machinery they must constrain has
already been built up.

@sec-interpretability begins inside the model, where neurons rarely mean one
thing and sparse dictionaries offer both a handle and a distortion. @sec-oversight-control
asks what to do when the system being judged can outpace the judge, splitting the
field into trust-building and containment approaches. @sec-security-authorization
then moves to permissions, credentials, and the verb every tool call eventually
performs. @sec-runtime-safety and @sec-adversarial-robustness deal with behavior
at the boundary: guardrails, classifiers, jailbreaks, red teams, and the fact
that a refusal is only a soft wall. @sec-privacy-provenance and @sec-law-policy
add the promises made to data subjects, rights holders, users, regulators, and
the public.

The part is deliberately broad because the failure modes are broad. There is no
single safety switch. The useful map is where evidence is created, where
authority is granted, where a policy becomes code, and where a claim of control
can actually be tested.

## Part reflection

- **Covered:** Mechanistic interpretability, scalable oversight, permissions and authorization, runtime safety, adversarial robustness, privacy, provenance, unlearning, law, regulation, and policy.
- **Main concern:** Safety claims often live at different layers from the evidence that would support them; a policy sentence, a classifier, a permission boundary, and a legal duty do not control the same thing.
- **Takeaway:** A safety mechanism is credible only when its evidence, authority, enforcement point, and failure mode are located in the stack.
- **Open question:** How should governance adapt when models gain more autonomy, tool access, and cross-border deployment while the technical evidence remains incomplete?
